Knowledge Distillation: A Practitioner's Note
=============================================

Motivation
----------
Modern neural networks are powerful but expensive to deploy. A model
that fits comfortably on a research workstation may be too slow or too
memory-hungry for an embedded device. Knowledge distillation (Hinton,
Vinyals, Dean, 2015) addresses this gap by training a small "student"
network to mimic the output of a large "teacher" network.

Soft Targets
------------
The key insight is that the teacher's output distribution carries
information that hard labels lose. A teacher trained on ImageNet may
assign a probability of 0.92 to "Labrador retriever" and 0.03 to
"golden retriever" for a single image. The 0.03 implicitly encodes
that goldens look more like Labradors than they do like trucks. By
training the student to match this distribution, the student inherits
that inter-class structure.

To make those small probabilities visible the softmax is computed at
temperature T > 1:

    p_i = exp(z_i / T) / sum_j exp(z_j / T)

Larger T flattens the distribution and exposes the relative ranking
of the non-top classes.

Loss
----
The student is trained with a weighted sum of two terms:

    L = alpha * KL(softmax(z_s / T) || softmax(z_t / T)) * T^2
      + (1 - alpha) * CE(softmax(z_s), y)

where z_s and z_t are the student and teacher logits, y is the ground
truth, and alpha trades off teacher imitation against task accuracy.
The T^2 factor keeps the gradient magnitude comparable to the
hard-label term when T is raised.

Results
-------
Across vision and language benchmarks, students recover most of the
teacher's accuracy at a fraction of the parameter count and inference
cost. Modern production stacks routinely ship distilled variants of
their flagship models on mobile and edge hardware.

References
----------
Hinton, G., Vinyals, O., & Dean, J. (2015). Distilling the Knowledge
in a Neural Network. arXiv:1503.02531.
